consensus_summary: All four blind responses agree that 'Gospel' (euangelion) means the good news of salvation accomplished through Jesus Christ's death, burial, and resurrection, with 1 Corinthians 15:1-4, Romans 1:16, and Mark 1:14-15 as defining texts. Every response also lists a common alternative: the gospel as the announcement of the kingdom/reign of God, rooted in Isaiah 52:7, alongside the literary sense (the four canonical books) and minority social-liberation readings. The consensus treats kingdom and cross-resurrection emphases as complementary accents on the same referent.
book_summary: The book defines the gospel as the message of the coming kingdom in which the law goes forth from Zion (Isa 2:3), a message proclaimed beforehand to Abraham (Gen 12:3; Gal 3:8) and to Israel at Sinai (Heb 4:2), and renewed under Jesus' rule. Its common-view note explicitly flags the standard definition — Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose — as what is 'commonly taught,' positioning its own kingdom-and-law-centered definition as the correction or fuller account.
consensus_core_identification: The good news of salvation in Christ's death and resurrection (with the inaugurated kingdom of God as a recognized complementary emphasis).
book_core_identification: The good news of a coming kingdom under Jesus' rule in which the law goes forth from Zion — a message preached before Christ to Abraham and at Sinai, and thus not defined by Christ's death and resurrection.
boundary_disagreement: The book relocates the gospel's center from the death-burial-resurrection kerygma to the future kingdom and Torah-from-Zion, and extends the gospel's instances backward to include the promise to Abraham and the proclamation at Sinai as genuine gospel preaching. The consensus's kingdom reading is inaugurated (in-breaking in Jesus' ministry), whereas the book's kingdom is 'coming' and law-centered, an eschatological/restorationist framing. The consensus's defining content (1 Cor 15:1-4) is demoted to a 'commonly taught' view rather than the gospel's core.
material_contradiction: None strictly stated: the book does not deny Christ's death and resurrection, and 'gospel of the kingdom' is a common alternative in every consensus response. But the book's common-view note implies the atonement-centered definition is inadequate as the gospel's identification, which presses toward contradiction without formally asserting it.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus category — the gospel as a proclaimed message of good news tied to God's saving reign — and its kingdom framing is explicitly listed as a common alternative in all four blind responses (Mark 1:14-15; Isa 52:7 background). However, it materially reworks boundaries: it adds pre-Christian proclamations (Abraham, Sinai) as instances of the gospel, makes the future law-from-Zion kingdom the defining content, and displaces the death-resurrection kerygma from the center. This is real boundary and emphasis disagreement within a recognized referent, not a replacement of the referent itself, so REFINED rather than DIVERGENT is the correct classification.
strongest_objection: One could argue DIVERGENT: by relegating 'Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again' (1 Cor 15:1-4) to a merely 'commonly taught' view, the book effectively replaces the consensus's defining content, and accepting the book's definition as THE gospel arguably requires rejecting the consensus identification of its core content, not just adjusting its boundary. Galatians 3:8 and Hebrews 4:2 genuinely support gospel preaching to Abraham and at Sinai, but the identification of that gospel's content as 'law going forth from Zion' rests on Isaiah 2:3, which never uses gospel language — an inferential link the printed citations alone do not secure.
